title: Level 1 - Registering Users with Email and Password
summary: Builds the simplest possible authentication: a users table in Postgres, a register route that checks for an existing email then inserts email and password, and a login route that compares the submitted password with the stored one. Works, but stores passwords as plain text, which is the weakness the next levels address.

concepts.heading: Starting project and prerequisites
points: Download and unzip the starter, cd into it, run npm i. Dependencies: body-parser, ejs, express, pg. Start with nodemon index.js and open localhost:3000.
Assumes prior modules on Express, EJS and PostgreSQL; the lesson does not re-teach them.

Pages: home (Login and Register buttons), login, register, and secrets.ejs, a plain page with a heading and a paragraph holding the secret. secrets.ejs is the protected page, to be rendered only after a successful register or login.
GET routes already just render the pages. The work is in the two POST routes, app.post('/register') and app.post('/login').

Leave the views alone, but note the form details: both forms use action pointing at their route, method POST, and two inputs named username (holds the email) and password. Those name attributes decide the keys on req.body.
The starter already has app.use(bodyParser.urlencoded({ extended: true })); Express's built-in express.urlencoded would work equally.

concepts.heading: Step 1: read the form data
points: Exercise: in both POST routes console.log the submitted values. Use req.body.username and req.body.password.
Before the fix both are undefined; after it the values appear in the terminal.

Then rename the local variable to email (const email = req.body.username). Only the right-hand side must match the form's name attribute; the left-hand name is free, and renaming helps tell form fields apart from server variables.
Delete the console.logs afterwards (they print passwords).

concepts.heading: Step 2: create the database and table
points: In pgAdmin: right-click Databases, create a database named secrets, open the Query Tool on it and run the CREATE TABLE from queries.sql.
id is SERIAL PRIMARY KEY (auto-generated). email is VARCHAR NOT NULL UNIQUE so no two users share an address. password is a plain VARCHAR.
Refresh Schemas > Tables and use View All Rows to see the empty table.
In index.js: import pg from 'pg', create new pg.Client with user postgres, host localhost, database secrets, your password, port 5432, then call db.connect().

concepts.heading: Step 3: register route
points: Naive version: db.query('INSERT INTO users (email, password) VALUES ($1, $2)', [email, password]) then res.render('secrets.ejs'). $1 and $2 are placeholders filled from the array, which keeps values out of the SQL text.
Registering the same email twice throws a duplicate key error from the UNIQUE constraint. That error is desirable, but it has to be handled.

Fix: first SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1. If checkResult.rows.length > 0 the user already exists, so respond with a message (send text, render a page, show a message) telling them to log in. Otherwise insert. A more elaborate site could log the user in automatically instead.
Wrap the queries in try/catch because pg calls can fail (no connection, wrong address or password, database gone); log or handle the error.
Verify by registering and viewing rows in pgAdmin: a new row with the email and password should appear.

concepts.heading: Step 4: login route
points: Within try/catch, SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1 with the submitted email.
result.rows is an array; because emails are unique it has at most one element. result.rows[0] is an object like {id, email, password}. Logging result.rows is a quick way to see this shape.

If rows.length > 0: take user = result.rows[0], storedPassword = user.password, compare it with the submitted password. Match: res.render('secrets.ejs'). Mismatch: tell them the password is wrong (or redirect to login, or flash a message).
Else (zero rows): no such user, tell them to register or check the email.

concepts.heading: Why this level is weak
points: Passwords sit readable in the table. Anyone who reads the database (breach, insider, backup leak) gets every email and password pair, and people reuse them across sites.
Subsequent levels add encryption, hashing and salting.

task.name: Level 1 authentication: register and log in
task.starting_point: Starter project with package.json, index.js (GET routes done, POST routes empty), views including secrets.ejs, queries.sql.
task.goal: Users can register (saved to Postgres) and log in with email and password to reach secrets.ejs.
steps: npm i, run nodemon index.js, visit localhost:3000.
In both POST routes, log req.body.username and req.body.password until they print; then rename to email and password and remove logs.
Create the secrets database and users table in pgAdmin using queries.sql.
Import pg, create the client, connect.
Register: SELECT by email; if found, send an 'already exists' message; else INSERT with $1/$2 and render secrets.ejs; wrap in try/catch.
Login: SELECT by email; if no row, say user not found; if row, compare passwords; render secrets.ejs on match, else say incorrect password.
Test: register, check row in pgAdmin, try re-registering, log in with right and wrong password.
task.expected_result: New users appear in the table; duplicate registration is rejected with a message; correct credentials show the secrets page, wrong ones a rejection message.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 35 - Authentication and Security - Handling Credentials & Designing a Secure Login/35.02 Level 1 - Registering Users with Email and Password

pitfalls: Reading req.body.email instead of req.body.username: the field is named username in the form, so it is undefined.
Duplicate email without a prior check crashes the insert with a unique-constraint error.

(Extra) The reference index.js has stray bugs: db.query not awaited in register, render imported from ejs and called instead of res.render, so the response never gets sent; the solution.js file fixes both. Use res.render and await.
(Extra) Plain text password storage and comparison with === is only acceptable for this teaching level.
(Extra) Echoing different messages for 'user not found' versus 'wrong password' lets attackers discover which emails are registered.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Level 1 login': blurb on register/login with a database; tasks: (1) read form values from req.body, (2) write the users CREATE TABLE with UNIQUE email, (3) check-then-insert register, (4) login compare, (5) spot the security problem. Starter: Express app with an in-memory users array and the two forms. Interactive demo: in-browser fake users table where registering adds a row showing the plaintext password, highlighting the leak risk.
